analysis.one_liner: Bars landlords from filing evictions for unpaid rent and from charging late fees, for all renters, until March 2021.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote: it was referred to two House committees on June 29, 2020 and no further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would replace the CARES Act's eviction moratorium, which protected only tenants in federally assisted housing and was set to lapse on July 25, 2020, with a moratorium covering every renter in the country until March 27, 2021. It would stop landlords from filing eviction cases for nonpayment and from charging late fees or penalties tied to unpaid rent during that period. After the moratorium ended, landlords would have to give tenants a 30-day notice before requiring them to leave for nonpayment.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who fell behind on rent because of pandemic job losses — the bill's own findings note more than 40 million unemployment filings since the pandemic began [S3]. It covered every renter household, not just those in federally assisted housing, so the roughly 36% of U.S. households that rent would be protected from eviction filings and late fees for nine extra months [S3]. It also protected renters in the months after the moratorium by requiring a 30-day notice to vacate for nonpayment [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Extends eviction protections to all tenants, rather than only tenants of federally assisted properties, as the CARES Act did [S2].
Runs the moratorium for one year beginning March 27, 2020 — until March 27, 2021 — while the existing moratorium was set to expire July 25, 2020 [S2].
Bars landlords from filing court actions to recover possession for nonpayment of rent or fees, and from charging fees, penalties, or other charges related to nonpayment, during the moratorium [S3].
After the moratorium expires, landlords cannot require a tenant to leave for nonpayment until 30 days after giving notice to vacate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords, who could not file evictions for unpaid rent or collect late fees during the moratorium. The bill offers them no compensation or offsetting relief, so property owners — especially smaller ones carrying mortgages, taxes, and upkeep — would absorb the missed rent during the covered period, and unpaid balances would accumulate as debt to be collected later [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no rental assistance or compensation for landlords; missed rent does not disappear, it accumulates as debt owed by tenants after the moratorium ends, and landlords remain on the hook for mortgages, taxes, and maintenance in the meantime [S3].
A blanket moratorium applies regardless of a landlord's own financial situation, which hits small landlords without reserves harder than large institutional owners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For renters facing pandemic income loss, the bill addressed a direct, urgent harm: losing a home in the middle of a public health crisis, which the bill's findings argue would increase homelessness and undercut pandemic containment [S3]. The real cost is that unpaid rent is deferred, not forgiven, and landlords bear it without offsetting relief — a gap that could be filled by rental assistance instead. On balance, the protection it offered renters was substantial and the cost to landlords was a temporary deferral, though the design would have been stronger paired with aid to property owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced June 29, 2020 and referred to both the Financial Services and Judiciary Committees, but neither committee ever took it up, so it died without a markup or a vote in either chamber [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia of Illinois introduced the bill on June 29, 2020, joined by 30 Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Pressley, Tlaib, Ocasio-Cortez, Jayapal, Waters, and Nadler [S3][S4].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary — a split referral that gave either committee jurisdiction over its provisions [S5].
No committee markup, hearing, floor vote, or further action of any kind followed; the bill's entire recorded history is the introduction and referral on June 29, 2020 [S5].
The existing CARES Act moratorium it sought to replace applied only to tenants of federally assisted properties and expired on July 25, 2020 [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners, who kept full freedom to file evictions and charge fees after the narrower federal moratorium expired July 25, 2020; renters outside federally assisted housing got no nationwide protection from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 29, 2020 to extend the eviction moratorium to all tenants through March 27, 2021 [S3][S5].

for.name: 30 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, adding their names in support at introduction [S4].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral (chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 29, 2020 and never scheduled a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Additional committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 29, 2020 and never took any action on it before the Congress ended [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 31 supporters — the sponsor and 30 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored and no vote was ever taken, so no roll call records the split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar them from filing evictions for nonpayment and from charging late fees until March 27, 2021, covering all renters rather than only federally assisted properties. Because the bill provides no rental assistance, missed rent would accumulate as debt, but owners lose immediate collection and court remedies during the moratorium [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Eviction filing and collections ecosystem (process servers, courts, debt collectors)
industries.note: By prohibiting new eviction filings for nonpayment during the moratorium, the bill would cut off the pipeline of eviction cases and associated fees that this ecosystem processes [S3].
